title: Macbeth
author: William Shakespeare
sourceNote: Act 5, Scene 5 — the 'tomorrow and tomorrow' soliloquy
description: Written around 1606 for King James, who had a documented interest in witchcraft, and the shortest of Shakespeare's tragedies as it survives.

title: Hope is the thing with feathers
author: Emily Dickinson
description: Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems in near-total seclusion in Amherst, Massachusetts, and saw barely a handful published in her lifetime, always anonymously and against her preference.

title: The Tyger
author: William Blake
description: Blake engraved, printed, and hand-colored his own books himself, and paired this poem in Songs of Experience with its counterpart 'The Lamb' from the earlier Songs of Innocence.

title: Death, be not proud
author: John Donne
description: One of nineteen Holy Sonnets Donne wrote after turning from a youth of love poetry and litigation to the Anglican priesthood; none of them were published until after his death.

title: The Road Not Taken
author: Robert Frost
description: Frost wrote this for his friend Edward Thomas, who was known for agonizing over which path to take on their walks together; Thomas later died in the First World War, not long after enlisting.

title: Ode to a Nightingale
author: John Keats
description: Written a few months after Keats had nursed his younger brother Tom through his death from tuberculosis, the same disease that would kill Keats himself less than two years later.

title: Annabel Lee
author: Edgar Allan Poe
description: Poe's last completed poem, published just days after his death in 1849 under circumstances that remain unexplained; biographers have long debated which, if any, real woman it was written for.

title: O Captain! My Captain!
author: Walt Whitman
sourceNote: Leaves of Grass, written for Lincoln, 1865
description: Written within weeks of Lincoln's assassination in 1865, in conventional rhyme and meter unlike almost everything else Whitman wrote, which is part of why it became the most popular poem of his career against his own wishes.

title: Ulysses
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
description: Written in 1833, the same year Tennyson's closest friend Arthur Hallam died suddenly at twenty-two, an event that also produced Tennyson's long elegy In Memoriam over the following seventeen years.

title: Remember
author: Christina Rossetti
description: Rossetti wrote prolifically on death and renunciation throughout her life and later gave up much of her own writing to work at a refuge for former sex workers in Highgate.

title: Ozymandias
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
description: Written in a friendly competition with another poet, Horace Smith, who published his own sonnet on the same subject in the same year; Shelley's is the one that survived.

title: Hamlet
author: William Shakespeare
sourceNote: Act 3, Scene 1 — the 'to be, or not to be' soliloquy
description: Survives in three substantially different early printed texts, and this familiar wording comes from the Second Quarto and First Folio rather than the shorter, stranger First Quarto often called the 'bad quarto.'

title: Romeo and Juliet
author: William Shakespeare
description: Written early in Shakespeare's career, around 1594-96, and based on a long narrative poem by Arthur Brooke that was itself translated from an Italian tale already decades old by then.

title: Othello
author: William Shakespeare
description: Based on an Italian prose tale by Cinthio in which the characters are mostly unnamed, with the ensign (the source for Iago) given a far more mundane motive than anything Shakespeare supplies.

title: Twelfth Night
author: William Shakespeare
sourceNote: Act 1, Scene 1 — 'If music be the food of love'
description: Named for the twelfth night after Christmas, the end of the Elizabethan festive season when ordinary social rules were traditionally suspended for licensed misrule and disguise.

title: The Importance of Being Earnest
author: Oscar Wilde
sourceNote: Act 1 — Lady Bracknell's interrogation of Jack
description: Opened in London in February 1895 to immediate acclaim; within months Wilde's own trials began, and his name was removed from the playbill while it was still running.

title: Doctor Faustus
author: Christopher Marlowe
sourceNote: Act 5, Scene 1 — Faustus and the spirit of Helen
description: Marlowe was born the same year as Shakespeare, 1564, but was killed in a tavern brawl at twenty-nine, a decade before Shakespeare wrote his own best-known tragedies.

title: A Doll's House
author: Henrik Ibsen
description: Its original 1879 ending was so controversial that Ibsen, under pressure from a German producer, wrote an alternate conclusion he later called a disgrace he was forced into.

title: Julius Caesar
author: William Shakespeare
description: Drawn primarily from Thomas North's 1579 English translation of Plutarch's Lives, which Shakespeare followed closely enough in places to lift North's own phrasing almost directly.

title: As You Like It
author: William Shakespeare
sourceNote: Act 2, Scene 7 — 'All the world's a stage'
description: The seven-ages structure Jaques uses here draws on a much older idea found in classical and medieval writing, sometimes illustrated as a wheel or staircase of a person's life.

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
description: Austen originally titled an early draft of this novel First Impressions in the 1790s; it wasn't published, revised and retitled, until 1813, and anonymously at that.

title: Moby-Dick
author: Herman Melville
description: A commercial failure on publication in 1851 that effectively ended Melville's career as a popular novelist; its reputation was only rebuilt by critics decades after his death.

title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Brontë
description: Published in 1847 under the male pseudonym Currer Bell, a choice Charlotte Brontë later said she made because female authors risked being judged on their sex rather than their work.

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
description: Written when Mary Shelley was eighteen, begun as part of a ghost-story contest with Percy Shelley and Lord Byron during a rainy summer by Lake Geneva in 1816.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
description: First published in 1890 in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, which had already quietly cut roughly five hundred words the magazine's editor considered too suggestive before it ran.

title: A Tale of Two Cities
author: Charles Dickens
description: Set against the French Revolution some seventy years before Dickens wrote it, drawing partly on Thomas Carlyle's history of the period, which Dickens said he read repeatedly while writing.

title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad
description: Drawn heavily from Conrad's own brief, disillusioning stint captaining a steamboat on the Congo River in 1890, an experience he said left him changed for the rest of his life.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
description: Gilman wrote this partly in response to a real 'rest cure' doctor had prescribed her for depression, which forbade her from writing at all; she later said the story was meant to change his mind, and did.

title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë
description: Published in 1847 under the pseudonym Ellis Bell; Emily Brontë died the following year, having seen only this one novel into print.

title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker
description: Told entirely through letters, diary entries, and newspaper clippings, a format Stoker used to let multiple narrators describe the same events from incomplete and conflicting angles.
